title: tRPC: a first input that is an array, tuple or class instance, followed by a middleware, is typed as an object of its members, and four valid uses of it fail to compile at both commits
saved_outcome: T1 is advisory. It adds no causal family.

promise.whose_interface: tRPC's own: the types ProcedureBuilder gives a resolver and a caller for a whole input that is an array, a tuple or a class instance when .use() follows .input(). No dependency owns it; Zod only supplies the validator's declared type.
promise.source: The accepted type: `input<$Parser extends Parser>(schema: TParams['_input_out'] extends UnsetMarker ? $Parser : ...` in packages/server/src/core/internals/procedureBuilder.ts at the head takes any validator as the first input, and refuses only a second non-object input with "All input parsers did not resolve to an object". The project's own tests: `deletePosts: t.procedure.input(z.array(z.string()).nullish())` in packages/tests/server/react/__testHelpers.tsx line 118, and nine `.input(z.date())` procedures in packages/tests/server/transformer.test.ts. None has a middleware after the input.

(data-transformers.md line 8). The first two searches returned nothing: the documentation shows no array, tuple, date, set, map or class-instance input and does not use the words array or tuple under www/docs/server. The earlier count of inputs by type across docs, examples and tests is in K2/upstream/search-trpc-docs-tests-array-inputs.txt.

owner-docs.reason: tRPC owns the builder and the Overwrite helper that produce the type. No dependency owns the operation.

band_reason: Proposed, and decided separately. A build error in a developer's own resolver, with a workaround, that the change leaves in place and did not cause. GT-j4 and GT-j5, the two older compile failures from the same unchanged copy, were both ruled other-material.
rule_gap: Rule Delivered asks whether a person "in that use" gets the outcome and does not say whether one valid use that fails makes a promised input not delivered when its ordinary uses work. The claim on file covers arrays, tuples, dates, sets, maps and classes in one statement while the facts differ by input, so whether it is one claim or several is a grouping question for the owner, as is grouping with GT-j4 under rule Before 4 (same lines yes; no single narrow fix cures both; one sentence about the cause is true of both).

reproduced.base: Run with TypeScript 5.1.3: the resolver's and the caller's type of `.input(z.array(z.string())).use(mw)` is a 4,661 character object type; spreading a tuple input (TS2556), passing on a class instance with a private field (TS2345), Promise.all(input) and Object.values(input) (TS2322) fail to compile, and compile without the middleware. About 70 ordinary uses compile.
reproduced.head: The same, with identical error text.

not_run: the project's own test suite against any fix
an editor; the language service's hover text was taken
a type cast as the workaround for three of the four failing uses
strongest_argument_against: For the input the reviews named, a plain array, every ordinary use compiles and only the printed type is wrong. The failing uses are a tuple spread, a class with a private member and two unusual calls, nobody is shown writing them, no report was found in three years, the change neither caused nor worsened it, and its words are about strings. On that reading the saved claim stays a minor defect and the failing uses are a narrower thing no review raised. The code search adds that public programs do put a middleware after an array input, all found ones later than the cut-off, and none uses the input in a way that fails.
facts_new_since_the_saved_ruling: Four valid uses fail to compile at both commits with the middleware and compile without it (run).
The resolver's type for an array input with a middleware is the long object at release 10.43.0 as well; only the caller's type first went wrong in 10.43.1 (run).
The release note the saved reason cites is from after the last push; the other three sources it cites are from before it.
Five public files in five repositories put a middleware after an array input; all were first committed after the cut-off and none uses a failing use (read).

title: Django: with OPTIONS["pool"] on, a connection that cannot be opened or set up reaches the caller as a pool timeout after the wait, and the server's message is only in the pool library's log
saved_outcome: D7b is advisory. It adds no causal family.

promise.whose_interface: psycopg_pool's, a dependency: its background workers open and configure connections, retry failures and decide what a waiting caller is told. Django's part is handing its setup to the pool's configure callback, calling getconn() and wrapping the exception.

project-docs.query: On docs and django of django/django at the head fad334e1: rg -n -i 'pool' docs --glob '*.txt' (release notes before 5.0 and the words whirlpool and spool removed); rg -n -i 'PoolTimeout|couldn.t get a connection|psycopg\.pool|reconnect_failed|error connecting' docs django. A third search, for OperationalError, __cause__ and wrap_database_errors, is in K3/upstream/search-django-docs-connection-errors.txt (6 hits, all read)
project-docs.found: The pool section says only how to turn the option on: "to be a dict to be passed to :class:`~psycopg:psycopg_pool.ConnectionPool`, or to ``True`` to use the ``ConnectionPool`` defaults". The other pool lines are about Redis, PgBouncer and multi-database routing. The second search returned nothing: no page mentions the pool's timeout, its logger or how a failed connection is reported. The older exceptions page says "a ``__cause__`` attribute is set with the original (underlying) database exception, allowing access to any additional information provided."

documented-way.query: venv/bin/python probes/run_all.py <scratch>/head head <scratch>/sock 54431 with psycopg 3.1.18 and psycopg_pool 3.2.1 on PostgreSQL 16.15: the documented `"pool": True` and a pool dictionary, with right and wrong settings, and the same without the pool
documented-way.found: With right settings the documented option works: the first query returns at once. Without the pool the server's message is the exception, at once, at both commits. With the pool on and a wrong database, password, host or time zone the caller gets "couldn't get a connection after 6.00 sec" (30.00 by default), the server's message is not in the exception chain, and the pool library logs it at warning level on every attempt.

rule_gap: Rule Promised 4b counts a dependency's documentation for the features the project points to, and has no line for a dependency's documented limit. Rule Delivered 1's "a message a person needs" has no test for a message that is in the log and not in the exception. Whether the older sentence in Django's exceptions page, that __cause__ gives access to the original database exception's information, reaches an error raised on the pool's own thread is a reading for the owner. Django's ticket tracker could not be searched directly; it was reached through an index and by fetching tickets by number, and no promise is expected to live only there.

reproduced.base: The pool option does not exist: every case that sets it fails at once with 'invalid connection option "pool"'. Without it the server's message is the exception, at once.
reproduced.head: Pool on: OperationalError "couldn't get a connection after 6.00 sec" caused by psycopg_pool.PoolTimeout after the full timeout, for a rejected time zone, a missing database, a wrong password and a server that is down; the server's message is logged by psycopg.pool on each attempt and is absent from the exception chain. Pool off: unchanged from the base.

not_run: a web request through a server
a settings file with a real time zone the server lacks; the run set the zone through settings.configure()
strongest_argument_against: A new user who mistypes a password gets a 30 second wait and an error that says nothing about passwords, where the same mistake without the pool is answered at once in the server's words; a project that discards warnings sees no reason at all. If the owner reads Django's exceptions page as covering this, it is promised and not delivered, which is a problem and reopens ruling 44. If the owner counts pooling as promised use with a late, empty error as the thing wrong, it is a minor defect.
facts_new_since_the_saved_ruling: psycopg's pool documentation from before the cut-off describes this behaviour in words (read).
Run with the library versions from before the cut-off (psycopg 3.1.18, psycopg_pool 3.2.1), with a wrong password and a server that is down added, and under four logging configurations.
The maintainer's advice to enable pool logging, cited in the first-round dossier, is from 2024-10-01, after the cut-off. No reason of the saved ruling depends on it.
A code comment in the change says wrap_database_errors does not reach work the pool defers into a thread, said of the reset callback (read). It is not in the dossier or the case file.

Public code, all later than the cut-off: many Django projects catch or log PoolTimeout for pool exhaustion; one test (ang-ee/angee-django, 2026) asserts the timeout for an unreachable server as the expected behaviour; one project that uses psycopg_pool directly (tomcounsell/popoto, 2026) changed its own error to carry the last connection attempt's message, "because the pool connects in its own threads" (read).

title: Django: during a key rotation rolled out one server at a time, a visitor kept by a server with the new key is signed out by a server that has only the old key
saved_outcome: not promised. A suggestion or observation; it stays off the answer key. Nobody is shown depending on a staged rollout keeping sessions, so it is not of the kind relied on.
proposed_kind_before: suggestion, sub-kind outside supported use (kind stated by the owner; sub-kind proposed, confidence low)

promise.whose_interface: Django's own: get_user(), the session auth hash and the session backends. The operation is keeping a session usable on a server that lacks the key another server signed it with. No dependency owns it.

project-docs.query: On docs of django/django at the head 2396933c, three searches: rg -n 'SECRET_KEY_FALLBACKS' docs; rg -n -i 'rotat' docs --glob '!docs/releases/[0-3]*'; rg -n -i 'servers|nodes|instances|machines|load.?balanc|cluster|rolling|staged|zero.?downtime|blue.?green|one at a time|distributed' over the settings, signing, deployment checklist, auth and session pages and the 4.1, 4.1.8 and 4.2 release notes
project-docs.found: No passage about rotating the key mentions more than one server. What the documentation does say: "When a secret key is no longer set as :setting:`SECRET_KEY` or contained within :setting:`SECRET_KEY_FALLBACKS` all of the above will be invalidated."; "A list of fallback secret keys for a particular Django installation."; "In order to rotate your secret keys, set a new ``SECRET_KEY`` and move the previous value to the beginning of ``SECRET_KEY_FALLBACKS``." The 4.1 release notes, for another setting: "If you are upgrading multiple instances of the same project to Django 4.1, you should set ``CSRF_COOKIE_MASKED`` to ``True`` during the transition".

owner-docs.reason: Django owns session verification and the session backends. No dependency owns the operation.

documented-way.query: venv/bin/python probes/sequences.py <scratch>/head and <scratch>/base, then probes/compare.py: the documented recipe on all servers at once (path N, N), the recipe on one server at a time (N, O), and both keys sent to every server first (P, N, P), among 840 paths
documented-way.found: At the head the documented recipe applied to every server keeps the visitor signed in with the session's value (signed out before the change). Sending both keys to every server first keeps the visitor throughout. Applied one server at a time, the visitor is signed in at the switched server and signed out at the old-only one, where before the change they were signed out at the switched server. None of 840 paths ends worse after the change.

rule_gap: The table's first column, "Does something stop working?", does not say compared with what: against the commit before the change the answer is no, and read as "does this use fail" it is yes. Decision P28 names a kind when the owners said a use is unsupported and when they never spoke and someone is shown doing it; here they never spoke and nobody is shown doing it. No line says whether documentation that states a limit in general terms counts as documenting that a use is unsupported. The search made after the dossier found two older tickets in which maintainers speak of servers holding different keys (20081, 2013, and 31864, 2020). They are general and predate the fallback setting. If the table's first column is read as "does this use fail", they bear on decision P28's first test; if it is read against the commit before the change, they do not change the sub-kind.

reproduced.base: Cache sessions: a visitor signed in before the switch is signed out, and the session deleted, at the first server that has the new key.
reproduced.head: The same visitor stays signed in at the server with the new key and is signed out, and the session deleted, at a server that has only the old key. With database sessions the old-only server treats the visitor as anonymous and deletes nothing.

strongest_argument_against: Django's documentation says that when a key "is no longer set as SECRET_KEY or contained within SECRET_KEY_FALLBACKS all of the above will be invalidated", which describes the old-only server exactly, and its rotation recipe is written for "a particular Django installation". If the owner reads that as the owners having documented the limit, decision P28's first test is met and the sub-kind is outside supported use, as the earlier dossier said. A maintainer's words of 2024, "the docs seem to assume a single-node deployment", agree, but came after the cut-off. A ticket of 2013 has project members calling differing secrets across web nodes "bad news", which is the owners speaking, in general terms, before the cut-off.
facts_new_since_the_saved_ruling: 840 paths compared at both commits, none worse after the change (run).
Django's release notes for 3.1 and 4.1 tell sites "upgrading multiple instances of the same project" what to set during a transition; nothing comparable exists for key rotation (read).
No statement about several servers in the pull requests and ticket that introduced the setting or on the Django forum before the cut-off (read).
Found after the dossier and the case file were written, and in neither: ticket 20081 (2013 to 2014) and ticket 31864 (2020), quoted under promise.searched.maintainers (read).

Public documents, all first committed in 2026: two say a rolling fleet needs the new key sent to every server before the switch; two say Django's fallbacks allow rotation through a rolling update. No program is shown depending on sessions surviving the mixed state (read).
